🛜 🌍 The world's biggest domain seller GoDaddy says India's fight against fake websites could make the internet less safe. A fight not many are watching,  but is set to reshape internet governance, we report at @Reuters 

🌍Let's understand the background -- India has a fake-website problem. For years, fraudsters have registered domains impersonating global brands -- bogus Amazon shopping sites, fake McDonald's franchise offers, phony Microsoft support pages -- to con ordinary people. Dozens of companies took them to court.

🌍 What happened in December 2025? a Delhi judge cracked down. She blocked more than 1,100 fraudulent sites. But she didn't stop there.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

🌍 The big news now: Now GoDaddy -- which runs 80 million domains worldwide -- is fighting back in thousands of pages of court filings my colleagues and I reviewed . Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

🌍 It's a landmark collision between a nation trying to protect its citizens and the borderless architecture of the internet itself.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network

3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Mahatma Gandhi — The Man Who Died, But Whose Ideas Refused to Die
Mahatma Gandhi was not born a Mahatma. He became one through a lifetime of mistakes, self-discipline, courage, experiments with truth and an extraordinary commitment to humanity.
Born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi grew up in a deeply religious environment. He went to London to study law and later travelled to South Africa, where the experience of racial discrimination transformed his understanding of injustice. There, Gandhi developed Satyagraha — the idea that truth and non-violent resistance could challenge oppression without hatred.
When he returned to India, he did not simply become a politician. He became a voice for ordinary Indians — farmers, workers, women, the poor and those pushed to the margins of society. From Champaran and Kheda to the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Salt March and the Quit India Movement, Gandhi turned political struggle into a mass movement.
His greatest strength was not physical power. It was moral courage.
He taught that fearlessness does not mean hatred, that strength does not require violence, and that freedom without responsibility is incomplete. He wore simple clothes while standing before the might of the British Empire. He walked among ordinary people while becoming known across the world. His simplicity itself became a form of power.
But Gandhi was not a flawless man. He made mistakes, changed his views, questioned himself and constantly experimented with his own beliefs. That is precisely why his life remains worth studying: he showed that becoming a better human being is a lifelong struggle.
The final years of Gandhi's life were among his most painful. Partition brought horrific communal violence. While many sought political power, Gandhi walked through areas affected by Hindu-Muslim violence, fasting and appealing for peace. He believed India could not truly be free if Indians learned to hate one another.
On 30 January 1948, Gandhi was assassinated in New Delhi by Nathuram Godse. The assassination shook the nation. The Government of India subsequently arrested members of the RSS and banned the organisation; the ban was lifted in July 1949 after the government received assurances and a written constitution addressing its stated conditions.
But here lies the deepest lesson.
A bullet can kill a human being. It cannot automatically kill an idea.
Gandhi's body fell, but his questions survived:
Can we disagree without hatred?
Can religion coexist with humanity?
Can political power remain accountable?
Can the weak stand against the powerful without becoming cruel themselves?
Can we fight injustice without becoming unjust?
These questions belong to every generation.
Gandhi should not be remembered merely because his photograph hangs in government offices or because political leaders pay tribute to him on anniversaries. Respect for Gandhi is not proved by garlands, speeches or photographs.
Respect for Gandhi is proved by conduct.
If we truly remember him, we must practise truth when lying would be easier, compassion when hatred is fashionable, courage when speaking up is dangerous, and non-violence when anger demands revenge.
Political leaders and parties may invoke Gandhi for their own reasons, and citizens are entitled to examine whether their actions reflect the principles they publicly honour. But Gandhi's legacy should be bigger than any party, government or election.
We do not remember Gandhi because he was powerful.
We remember him because he showed that a person without an army can still challenge an empire.
He was shot, but his philosophy survived.
His body was silenced, but his questions remained.
His life ended, but the struggle for truth, justice, dignity, communal harmony and human freedom did not.
Gandhi is not merely a portrait on a wall.
Gandhi is a question standing before every generation:
What will you do when truth demands courage?

Tired of poor government service or harassment by banks? CPGRAMS (Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System) is your direct line to the Govt of India to fix it.

Here is everything you need to know about how to use it effectively.

What can you complain about?
You can lodge complaints against 80+ Central Ministries & State Govts for:
• Delays in passports, Aadhaar, or PAN cards
• EPFO / PF withdrawal issues
• Non-payment of pensions
• Unresolved issues with railways, telecom, or posts.

Bank Recovery Harassment?
Yes, you can file it here! CPGRAMS routes banking & NBFC complaints to the Department of Financial Services (DFS).
• Report illegal recovery agent calls (outside 8 AM – 7 PM)
• Report threats, abuse, or unauthorized data sharing.

What CANNOT be registered?
CPGRAMS will automatically reject your case if it involves:
• Sub-judice matters (cases active in court)
• RTI applications or appeals
• Personal service matters of government employees
• General political suggestions

How it functions:
1️⃣ You register on https://t.co/6NYHqQZ1ir or the UMANG app.
2️⃣ File a complaint & select the relevant Ministry.
3️⃣ The portal acts as an administrative tracker, sending your case down to the designated department officer for resolution.
4️⃣ You get a 16-digit tracking ID.

Pros & Cons:
✅ Pros: 100% free, forces government departments to respond, and offers an internal appeal option if you get a poor resolution.

❌ Cons: It is purely administrative (has no judicial powers). It cannot overturn an RBI Ombudsman ruling or award court damages.

Jack Dorsey’s decentralized messaging app Bitchat has become largely unavailable in India after government action against the service.

Apple removed Bitchat from the India App Store following a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Reports say the removal was issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, which allows the government to block online content and services under certain conditions. (Moneycontrol)

Bitchat is designed to work without traditional internet infrastructure by using Bluetooth mesh networking. That allows nearby devices to communicate directly, making the app potentially useful during internet outages or shutdowns.

The Indian government had already targeted Bitchat earlier this year. In July, authorities sought restrictions on several of the project’s GitHub repositories, arguing that its anonymous and decentralized architecture could make lawful interception, attribution, and investigation more difficult. (TechCrunch)

The issue gained additional attention after Bitchat downloads surged during protests and internet restrictions in India. TechCrunch reported that India accounted for roughly 85% of the app’s global downloads during one week in July, with more than 91,000 downloads in five days. (TechCrunch)

As of October 3, Bitchat was also unavailable on Google Play in India, while its website was inaccessible during checks by local media. (Moneycontrol)

The dispute highlights a broader tension between decentralized communication tools and governments seeking to maintain the ability to monitor or restrict communications during emergencies and public unrest.

🔒 VPN BAN / RESTRICTION WATCHLIST - Oct 2026

🇧🇾 Belarus - VPN use is restricted/illegal under the country's internet-control regime.
🇮🇶 Iraq - VPNs are prohibited/restricted, with authorities targeting circumvention tools.
🇰🇵 North Korea - VPN access is effectively prohibited as part of total internet controls.
🇹🇲 Turkmenistan - VPNs are prohibited and authorities actively block VPN services.
🇲🇲 Myanmar - Unauthorized VPNs are illegal. Cybersecurity Law + arrests/phone checks.
🇮🇷 Iran - Unlicensed VPN use prohibited since 2024; only government-approved VPNs are permitted.
🇨🇳 China - VPNs aren't simply “illegal”: unauthorized VPN services/use are heavily restricted, and the Great Firewall blocks VPN infrastructure. Approved corporate VPNs remain possible.
🇷🇺 Russia - No blanket criminal ban on ordinary VPN use, but 469+ VPNs blocked by Feb 2026, VPN advertising banned, and blocking intensified in 2026.🇹🇷 Türkiye - VPN services are heavily restricted/blocked intermittently rather than there being a simple blanket consumer VPN ban.
🇮🇳 India - No nationwide VPN ban, but authorities have imposed local temporary VPN prohibitions, including districts in Jammu & Kashmir.
🇦🇪 UAE - VPNs are legal for legitimate purposes, but misuse to circumvent UAE laws can trigger criminal penalties.
🇺🇬 Uganda - VPN access has been restricted during political/internet-control periods, including the 2026 election period.
🇺🇸 Utah, USA - UPDATE: a federal judge blocked Utah's VPN-targeting age-verification provisions in Sept 2026. Not a VPN ban anymore.

Russia: Human Rights Watch reported that at least 469 VPNs had been blocked by February, with another wave of infrastructure blocking affecting roughly 20 providers in summer 2026.

Myanmar is also much more than a technical block: its 2025 Cybersecurity Law restricts unauthorized VPNs, while authorities have reportedly detained people over VPN use.

In Utah the federal court's preliminary injunction stopped the provisions aimed specifically at VPN circumvention.

This week, 119 nations gathered in Abu Dhabi and adopted the Abu Dhabi Declaration a five-year global roadmap for crime prevention and criminal justice. Adopted by acclamation. More than 40 ministers of justice in the room. The largest gathering of criminal justice policymakers on earth.

Abu Dhabi. The United Arab Emirates.

The same UAE where Golden Global Bank was designated for converting Iranian oil revenues to cash and gold for the Revolutionary Guard. The same UAE where Spain dismantled the Banca de Dubái a $2 billion crypto narcobank routing European cocaine money. The same UAE where Saudi Arabia's central bank secretly flagged bank transfers as high-risk. The same UAE that extradited Daniel Kinahan one of Europe's most wanted drug lords. The same UAE that arrested a Swedish money laundering fugitive linked to contract killings and handed evidence to INTERPOL.

That country just hosted 119 nations agreeing on how to fight crime for the next five years.

Here's what they committed to.

The Declaration has four pillars: prevention and resilience, justice and the rule of law, countering evolving crime threats, and international cooperation and innovation.

Under those pillars, 119 countries agreed to dismantle scam centers. The same scam centers this framework has been tracking Xinbi, which processed $36 billion. Huione, which was designated and dismantled in Operation Riptide. The compounds in Cambodia, Myanmar, Laos, and Madagascar where trafficked workers are forced to run online fraud operations. A sitting Cambodian senator was designated by U.S. Treasury this month for operating one. The Abu Dhabi Declaration now gives 119 nations the mandate to go after the rest.

They agreed to intensify cross-border cooperation on money laundering, terrorism financing, and asset recovery. The same cooperation that produced the INTERPOL Americas Conference 27 nations with binding AML commitments in Guyana two days before this congress opened.

They agreed to promote the responsible use of artificial intelligence in criminal justice while confronting criminals who use AI for cybercrime, fraud, trafficking, and terrorism financing. The same week the U.S. and China formalized the USA China AI Dialogues with a crisis hotline and a meeting scheduled in Shenzhen.

They agreed to consider treating crimes that harm the environment as serious crimes prosecutable under the same frameworks used against transnational organized crime. That means illegal logging, wildlife trafficking, and pollution can now trigger the same asset-seizure and money-laundering machinery as drug trafficking or sanctions evasion.

And they launched Pledge4Justice where individual countries make specific, time-bound commitments that will be tracked and published on the UNODC website through 2031. Not a statement of principles. An accountability mechanism. Public. Measurable. Five years.

The 16th congress will be hosted by Uzbekistan in 2031.

Now step back.

In one month:

27 nations sat in a room in Guyana and adopted binding AML enforcement commitments across the Western Hemisphere.

119 nations sat in a room in Abu Dhabi and adopted a five-year global anti-crime blueprint covering AI, scam centers, money laundering, terrorism financing, asset recovery, and environmental crime.

The U.S. and China formalized an AI governance framework with a hotline and a follow-up meeting in Shenzhen.

The U.S. and Russia met at the Kremlin with the acting head of OFAC in the room.

A U.S. Attorney flew to Guatemala with FBI, HSI, and DEA to formalize joint cartel prosecution.

Turkey revoked Iran's 44-year banking pipeline and started prosecuting its own ruling party for financial manipulation.

The UAE extradited drug lords, arrested fugitives, shared evidence with European police, and then hosted 119 nations to write the rules for doing it everywhere.

One month. Every continent. Every corridor. Every level from a grocery store in Detroit to the United Nations in Abu Dhabi.

The switchboard didn't just clean itself. It became the venue.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

On September 4, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned a small Turkish bank for moving Iranian oil money to the Revolutionary Guard.

Three weeks later, Turkey is tearing itself apart.

Here's what happened in order.

September 4  Treasury designated Golden Global Bank in Istanbul. The bank was set up to receive Iranian oil revenues from China and convert them to cash and gold for the IRGC. Treasury Secretary Bessent called it "code for you are out of business."

September 16  The Turkish stock market crashed. Regulators discovered suspected share-price manipulation across multiple investment fund companies. Seven companies managing 131 funds with $17 billion in assets were placed into liquidation.

September 18 Turkey's banking regulator quietly revoked the license of Iran's Bank Mellat one of the largest Iranian banks, operating in Turkey for 44 years. No press conference. No announcement. Just a line in the Official Gazette. The same week, Turkey grounded Iran's Mahan Air.

September 26  The deputy chairwoman of Erdogan's ruling party resigned after allegations that she and her husband sold tens of millions of dollars in shares before the stock market crash. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor launched legal proceedings against 76 people connected to the fund scandal. The ruling party's spokesman said: "All those who are involved in irregularities, corruption, abuse or anything that causes harm will be held accountable."

Three weeks. One country. Everything at once.

Iran's 44-year banking pipeline severed. Iran's military airline grounded. $17 billion in corrupt investment funds  liquidated. The ruling party's own deputy chair resigned and under investigation. 76 people facing prosecution.

That's the pattern.

Treasury hits a country from the outside. The country looks at the message. Then the country starts cleaning from the inside not just the thing Treasury targeted, but everything connected to it. Because once you start pulling the thread, everything attached to it comes loose.

The UAE did the same thing. Treasury hit Dubai's banking corridor. The UAE started arresting fugitives, extraditing drug lords, sharing evidence with European police. A brigadier general went on the record saying they'd take action against anyone exploiting their territory.

Now Turkey. Treasury hit one bank. Turkey revoked an entire 44-year banking relationship, grounded an airline, crashed its corrupt fund sector, and started prosecuting members of its own ruling party.

The same pattern is running everywhere.

Russia convicted 60,000 officials in five years and seized $9.5 billion in property.

China is purging a quarter of its governing body. The chairman of their securities regulator convicted of selling access to the stock market. Fifty ministerial-level investigations this year alone.

Saudi Arabia detained 298 officials in a single sweep including senior military and interior ministry officers.

India doubled its enforcement raids. A single betting app case traced $11.3 billion in criminal proceeds.

The United States tripled its counterintelligence arrests and is running the largest sanctions campaign in history.

And now Turkey a NATO ally that spent years playing both sides is cleaning house in three weeks flat.

Each country calls it something different. Turkey calls it market integrity. China calls it party discipline. Russia calls it anti-corruption. Saudi calls it national security. America calls it enforcement.

But they're all doing the same thing. At the same time. In the same direction.

And each one started with a message from the outside that the country answered from the inside.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

text:
An open letter to all my countrymen.

Do you want India to remain a democracy? Then you must understand what Gyanesh Kumar, the CEC, and his bosses are doing in the so-called SIR.
They are violating the law.
-  As per Section 21 of the law, a special revision is to be undertaken only in special cases, for reasons to be recorded in writing in each case; and that also only in any constituency or part of a constituency. An order for intensive revision for the whole country was illegal. An exception allowed for special cases cannot become the rule. The Supreme Court order upholding the general SIR was wrong.
Another question is - who took the decision for SIR in the whole country? Was it the full commission; or only Gyanesh Kumar.
-  Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, provides that where the revision of an electoral roll is taken up, the electoral roll in force at the time of the issue of the notification of revision shall continue in effect till the completion of the revision. The revised electoral rolls become complete only after all the appeals filed against inclusion or deletion are disposed off. Where the appeals were still pending, the original Electoral roll which was valid on the date of notification was to be used. Contrary to this the new roll with deletions was used during the elections even though appeals against deletions were still pending. This was illegal.

-  Section 22 of the RP Act provides that the Electoral Registration Officer, and not anyone else, can remove a voter's name from the roll and that also only on the grounds listed in Section 22(a), (b), and (c); and only after a specific enquiry, after giving the concerned person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and only after appeals against his order are disposed off. Gyanesh Kumar removed the names of all the voters who had been listed by the ERO's after 2003, without any basis, without any enquiry, and without any show cause to the registered voters. This was blatantly illegal.
              The persons whose names were removed summarily had to apply as fresh voters in Form 6 and give evidence that they were eligible to be registered. This is a clear violation of the Supreme Court judgement in Lal Babu Hussain and Others v. Electoral Registration Officer and Others, [(1995) 3 SCC 100], which held that the enquiry authority or the objector and not the voter - must bring forth material evidence to back any claim that an enrolled voter be disqualified. And in such cases the voter must be asked to show cause why his name should not be removed on the basis of the grounds adduced by the enquiry officer. All this did not happen.

          The established jurisprudence is that the onus to prove that there are sufficient grounds for subjecting any person to a disability or punishment is on the
person or institution which is seeking to inflict the punishment. Here, Gyanesh Kumar has inverted the burden of proof. This is also against the law.

           Up to now, the efforts of the Government and the Election Commission have always been to enroll all eligible voters. It was a mission to deepen democracy and empower all citizens. This is the first time in history of the country that the mission is to disenfranchise people.

            Gyanesh Kumar added a new appendix to Form 6. He was not authorised to do so, as Form 6 is mandated by statutory rules. And he added this himself – against the views of the two election commissioners. The decisions of the commission are to be taken either unanimously – or by a majority. The majority was against the addition of the new appendix to the form. So the addition of the new appendix was against the decisions of the Commission itself. So why was it added? On whose orders? This was illegal. This appendix asks the applicant to state the serial number in the 2003 voter list on which their parents' names were listed. Where can an ordinary person – a young man of 18; access the 2003 roll in 2026? This stopped the registration of all young voters. BJP knows that young voters will not vote for it.

           Objections to inclusion of voters names in form 7 were filed in bulk. Who filed them? How were the forms accepted and acted upon when the persons who signed it did not appear?

           Names of 16 lac voters found valid by the ERO were not registered in Bengal because, it seems, the EC filed appeals against them. Why? On which grounds? Who authorised the Commission to file appeals? Two Election Commissioners say they did not do so. So the Commission did not authorise anyone to file appeals. Who did it? Gyanesh Kumar? These people were prevented from voting in the election.
 
             So the Election Commission and some people from a political party were acting in cahoots  to get bogus Form 7 objections filed in bulk and delete names?
 
             How were elections allowed to be held when the appeals of lakhs of voters were pending? The ECI and the Supreme Court have to answer. The appeals which have been decided show that 90% of the voters who were left out were valid.

            A ridiculous thing was brought up called "logical discrepancy". Gyanesh Kumar does not have any idea of how the poor live in India. Their children are not born in hospitals. They do not have birth certificates. They do not have calendars in their homes. When the BLO approached them to enroll them in the voter list they gave their estimated year of birth. Similarly, when their fathers' names were enrolled in the electoral roll, they gave their estimated year of birth. The dumb people in the Election Commission, under Gyanesh Kumar, said that any difference of less than 15 years between father and children would be a logical discrepancy justifying excluding their names. The “Logical Discrepancy” names were excluded without enquiry, contrary to sec 21 of the act.

             The largest number of exclusions have been the poor and the underprivileged, those without a voice. They were and are mostly away from their homes, earning their daily bread. Lakhs are working in faraway places/states. They could not and cannot afford to go back to their homes for a month to get their names registered. They will go hungry if they do not earn. They cannot fill the complicated forms. They do not have birth certificates and the papers. Why should they sacrifice their daily wages for a vote?

             The illegal immigrants are not affected. The first thing they do on entering India is to get their documentation made—Aadhaar card, ration card, etc. The earlier immigrants are their support systems. It is the poor Indian citizens who have been disenfranchised. The dumb people in the Election Commission and their bosses did not understand this. Or they wanted it this way.

              Gyanesh Kumar has made a digital electoral roll and empowered it to refuse addition of names because of “Logical discrepancy”. In the name of "Logical discrepancy", the names of millions of voters have not been included. This is against the law. The only authority designated by law to add or delete names and publish the electoral rolls is the Electoral Registration Officer. Contrary to this, the electoral roll was centralised and the revision happened centrally. This was illegal.

            Two Election Commissioners pointed out that the only people authorized to add or delete names – the ERO, the DEO and the CEO were not being allowed to access the voter list. In Goa, 97 electors were found by the ERO to be valid and fit for inclusion in the roll. They have not been able to add their names to the roll as yet.

             The centralisation of the voter list amendment is dangerous. It can be used to cut voters from booths which vote against NDA. Is this what happened?

            Deleting voters names before verification is a heinous offence, and Gyanesh Kumar is guilty thereof.

            13 crores names have been deleted by SIR so far. This is 13% of the voters, and SIR is not over. The difference between NDA and INDIA in the 2024 elections was only 3%. So the deletion have had and will have a material impact on the elections.

            The press note issued after the Commission meeting on 26th September confirms the illegalities mentioned above.

            Did Gyanesh Kumar commit all these illegalities himself or was he directed to do so by his bosses?

            The Opposition says that they will impeach Gyanesh Kumar. That is an exercise in futility. They just do not have the numbers. If they really want a remedy, they should file criminal cases against Gyanesh Kumar.

            The next step to be taken is that all opposition parties should unite and say that they will not participate in any election till the CEC and Election Commissioners' resign and the selection of their successors is as per the previous selection system, with the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and a sitting Supreme Court judge. Elections held in states while the appeals of lakhs of voters were pending must be set aside and fresh elections held. And the poll must be held by ballot not by EVMs because no electronic system has yet been invented which cannot be hacked. That is why none of the economically and digitally advanced countries use EVMs.

             If we want to preserve our democracy the whole country will need to be made aware and united.

            The reputation of the Supreme Court has been besmirched by the judgement on SIR. It is at par in infamy with the judgement upholding the emergency. Hon’ble Judges may please note.

            The procrastination on the challenge to the law on selection of Election Commissioners is also sending a bad message about the Supreme Court – as it is an open and shut case that the Election Commissioners should not be selected by the party in power; but by a neutral selection committee to ensure their neutrality.
Let us unite to save our democracy.
                                                                                    RK Singh
                             (IAS Retd. Ex Union Home Secretary)

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
WHEN CRITICISM DISAPPEARS, DEMOCRACY NEEDS ANSWERS

A troubling question is emerging around the removal of social-media content critical of those in power:

Who decides what gets taken down—and on what specific legal grounds?

Peek TV says one of its ground reports was removed following an order attributed to the Delhi Police. According to the video, the notice accused accounts of sharing edited or fake propaganda and attempting to incite protests, but the creators say it did not identify a specific violation in their report.

This is where transparency becomes essential.

Section 69A of the IT Act does provide a legal framework for blocking online information. But the Supreme Court's 2015 Shreya Singhal judgment upheld that framework subject to safeguards, including recorded reasons for blocking so that affected parties can challenge the decision.

And this is not merely a theoretical concern. In April 2026, the Delhi High Court directed authorities in another social-media blocking matter to identify the specific objectionable material and pass a reasoned order.

So the democratic demand is straightforward:

Show the order.
State the specific violation.
Provide the legal basis.
Allow the affected creator to challenge it.

If content is genuinely unlawful, due process should establish that.

If it is journalism, criticism or satire that has been wrongly removed, due process should protect it.

Either way, secretive or unexplained censorship weakens public trust.

A democracy should be strong enough to face criticism—and transparent enough to explain every restriction placed on speech.

QUESTION. VERIFY. DEMAND DUE PROCESS.

text:
Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

⚖️ 𝐋𝐀𝐍𝐃𝐌𝐀𝐑𝐊 𝐆𝐒𝐓 𝐈𝐓𝐂 𝐉𝐔𝐃𝐆𝐌𝐄𝐍𝐓 — 𝐌𝐀𝐉𝐎𝐑 𝐑𝐄𝐋𝐈𝐄𝐅 𝐀𝐆𝐀𝐈𝐍𝐒𝐓 𝐌𝐄𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐍𝐈𝐂𝐀𝐋 𝐑𝐄𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐒𝐀𝐋 𝐎𝐅 𝐈𝐓𝐂

In Shaurya Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab & Another & connected matters, CWP-34296-2024, pronounced on 01.10.2026, the Punjab & Haryana High Court has laid down an important framework for application of Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act.

✅ Validity of Section 16(2)(c) read with Section 155 upheld, but the provision cannot be used in isolation to automatically reverse ITC merely because the supplier failed to pay tax. The officer must examine the genuineness of the transaction and surrounding circumstances.

🚫 Supplier cancellation, nil/short tax payment or departmental alerts are only triggers for inquiry — they are not, by themselves, sufficient grounds for ITC denial.

🔍 Before proceeding against the buyer, the Department must examine the supplier, invoices, relevant tax period, nature of default and recovery action already taken against the supplier.

📑 Where fraud is alleged under Section 74/74A, the SCN itself must contain facts connecting the purchaser with such fraud; supplier-side fraud cannot simply be transferred to the recipient.

🧾 Though the purchaser bears the burden under Section 155, eligibility may be established through invoices, e-way bills, transport documents, weighbridge slips, stock/consumption records and proof of actual receipt of supplies.

💰 Double recovery is impermissible. Tax already recovered from/deposited by the supplier must be considered, along with permissible re-availment of ITC; importantly, the law applicable to the relevant tax period must be applied.

👂 Taxpayers are entitled to personal hearing and a reasoned speaking order; where third-party statements are relied upon, a request for cross-examination must be considered by a reasoned order.

🛑 For the pending batch, taxpayers at SCN stage were allowed 8 weeks to file supplementary replies/evidence, and the Court directed that no fresh coercive recovery action be taken until fresh decisions are passed.

📌 Key Takeaway: Section 16(2)(c) remains valid, but ITC cannot be reversed mechanically. Supplier default must be examined through proper investigation, taxpayer evidence and due process before liability is fastened on the purchaser.

Complete Judgment link: https://t.co/AzgJP04WiR

Supreme Court also upheld that the Form 6, as prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, sets out a framework of documentation.

Supreme Court has also upheld that hold that the documentation regime prescribed by the ECI represents a considered exercise of its administrative discretion in furtherance of its Constitutional mandate, and refuses to hold the documentation framework (Declaration framework as Annexure D in Form 6) as arbitrary or violative of
