text:
$ASTS - Elon Musk has lost the space mobile race before it even began.

Source: CE Noticias Financieras (Latin America)

The fiercest space race isn't about returning to the moon. It's about allowing you to make a TikTok or watch Netflix on your phone anywhere on the planet, from the salt flats of Atacama to the dunes of Khongor in the Gobi Desert. To make this happen, two radically different design philosophies are at war, and several companies are building the infrastructure needed to ensure that every phone on the planet is permanently connected to the Internet.

On one side is Elon Musk's SpaceX--and all the imitators that have followed in Starlink's wake. Their approach is to invade space with tens of thousands of satellites, creating a network of objects covering low Earth orbit. On the other side is a small Texas-based company called AST SpaceMobile, which believes it can provide better service with fewer than 100 satellites in space.

Both companies--along with Amazon and a handful of Chinese organizations--want to dominate global wireless communications. The satellite constellation with the fastest service, the widest coverage, the best compatibility with 5G mobile phones, and the lowest operating costs will dominate how we communicate in the coming years. The prevailing approach will have a serious impact not only on the future of the internet, but also on the health of our planet and the future of the internet and humanity in space.

A new era of space race

SpaceX, owner of Starlink, launched the first satellite in 2019, providing broadband Internet access to anyone with a large Starlink antenna and a modem on the ground. Since then, it has put more than 9,000 satellites into orbit. The company plans to have a constellation of 34,000 satellites. Following Starlink's initial launch, several competitors followed suit, including Jeff Bezos and his Kuiper constellation--now called Amazon Leo--and the Chinese, whose plans include up to 250,000 satellites.

But there is a fundamental problem with this megaconstellation design: Musk's plan for space internet is a flawed , wasteful, and dangerous game of orbital Russian roulette .

Scientists are concerned that Starlink's projected constellation of 34,400 satellites (which could reach up to 75,000) will cause irreparable damage to the atmosphere. A large-scale constellation also dramatically increases the possibility of a space collision that could start a catastrophic chain reaction, destroying orbital networks that are crucial to our survival as a species.

Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and spaceflight historian at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, has been documenting satellite launches in his Jonathan's Space Report newsletter. He believes there may be better ways to achieve global satellite coverage, if we need to do so. "Personally, I prefer a smaller number of larger satellites," he tells me in a telephone interview. "One reason is the risk of space collisions. If you have 10 times more satellites, you have 100 times more near misses. So, just from that point of view, consolidating into a smaller number of satellites seems more sensible."

The better and more efficient alternative

That's where Musk's biggest competitor comes in. AST SpaceMobile has developed direct-to-mobile technology that uses large satellites called BlueBirds. These machines use thousands of antennas to deliver broadband coverage directly to standard mobile phones, says company president Scott Wisniewski.

"This approach is remarkably efficient: we can achieve global coverage with approximately 90 satellites, not thousands or even tens of thousands as other systems require," Wisniewski tells me in an email. McDowell agrees that AST's approach--if it succeeds in meeting its goals--is the best, most efficient, and least wasteful path forward.

The key is the size and sophistication of its satellites. AST's first generation of commercial satellites, BlueBird 1-5, are deployed in a huge 64.4-square-meter array in space. Today, the company has five BlueBird 1-5 satellites operating in orbit, but its ambitions are much greater. On December 24, AST launched the first of its new-generation satellites from India--called Block 2--and it broke records. BlueBird 6 has a surface area of nearly 223 square meters, making it the largest single satellite in low Earth orbit. The company plans to launch up to 60 more by the end of 2026.

"This large surface area is essential for capturing weak signals from standard, unmodified mobile phones on the ground," explains Wisniewski. "It is, in essence, a single, extremely powerful and sensitive cell tower in the sky, capable of serving a huge geographic area... This design philosophy directly addresses the two biggest threats posed by the megaconstellation model." First, with only about 90 Block 2 satellites needed for global coverage, the absolute volume of material launched and removed from orbit is orders of magnitude less than the tens of thousands planned by SpaceX and others. With a lifespan of 7 to 10 years, AST satellites are designed to outlast Starlink satellites, which have a lifespan of about 5 years. This combination of factors dramatically reduces the potential for atmospheric pollution.

In addition, fewer satellites dramatically reduce the risk of orbital collisions. "Fewer satellites in orbit inherently reduces the likelihood of collisions and the creation of space debris, promoting a more sustainable orbital environment," says Wisniewski. It is a solution based on precision engineering rather than brute numerical force, a testament to a different way of thinking about the problem.

As McDowell says, from a space traffic perspective, "fewer and larger satellites is probably better." It is a design choice that prioritizes sustainability and risk mitigation. And the total cost, much lower in the case of AST.

A reckless brute force plan

The central idea behind Starlink's direct-to-mobile service is brute force. It's the digital equivalent of saturation bombing: saturating low Earth orbit with tens of thousands of relatively small, cheap, and disposable satellites. Each one acts like a small cell tower in the sky, talking to the phone in your pocket. Because they are in low orbit, latency is minimal and the signal is strong enough for a standard phone. It's a simple concept, but its elegance is deceptive. In reality, it has the elegance of a greasy sandwich.

The Starlink model is based on a constant cycle of replacement. After about five years, they are programmed to fall back to Earth, disintegrating upon reentry. This is where the first major problem arises .

"When they disintegrate, they don't just vanish," McDowell explains. "They turn into dust, alumina dust, aluminum oxide particles. These particles are very effective at destroying ozone."

The long-term effect of depositing tons of this material into the upper atmosphere every day is a terrifying unknown. We are, in effect, conducting an uncontrolled experiment on our own planet's protective layers. McDowell points out that while a single rocket launch causes temporary, localized damage to the ozone, the continuous reentry of thousands of satellites creates a persistent, global problem that has never been studied on this scale.

SpaceX aggressively dismissed these concerns in 2021 in a legal battle with Viasat, a rival satellite internet service for home, business, and military use. Its legal defense directly attacked the scientific premise that satellites create harmful amounts of aluminum oxide when they burn up. The company has been ignoring warnings about potential ozone depletion since 2024.

Musk has attempted to address light pollution. Faced with protests from the astronomical community over the brightness of its satellites, they iterated on their design. First came DarkSat, an experimental coating that proved ineffective. Then came VisorSat, a deployable sunshade that blocked light reflection on the brightest parts of the satellite.

Now, McDowell tells me, they are using a dielectric mirror film that reflects less light back to Earth. "They have made a significant effort to reduce brightness, and the newer Starlink satellites are substantially dimmer than the early ones," he admits. "But they are still bright enough to be a problem for large tracking telescopes like the Vera Rubin Observatory."

These mitigation efforts, while commendable, only address a relatively minor problem--light pollution--and do nothing to solve the more fundamental problems of atmospheric pollution and orbital saturation. The problem is compounded by the fact that everyone is now copying this model. Amazon's Project Leo plans to launch more than 3,200 satellites... Beijing and some Chinese companies were planning two separate megaconstellations, Guowang and G60 Starlink, with a total of nearly 26,000 satellites. "We are only at the beginning of this, " warns McDowell. "And that becomes very worrying because now it's not just one company, it's a lot of companies." To further increase his concerns, just a few days ago the Chinese government requested launch permits for 200,000 satellites.

AST's approach is not without its own controversies. The size of its satellites makes them very bright in the night sky, a major source of frustration for astronomers on the ground. McDowell confirms that when it was launched in 2022, AST's prototype satellite, BlueWalker 3, became "one of the ten brightest objects in the night sky for a while."

"It's a serious problem, and we're working directly with the astronomical community to mitigate our impact," Wisniewski tells me. The company is exploring solutions such as anti-reflective coatings and operational adjustments to minimize the time its satellites are at their brightest. However, McDowell is not aware of anyone working with AST SpaceMobile, and the latter did not provide any details.

According to McDowell, however, the size and brightness is a reasonable trade-off. "Even though the BlueBirds are bright, there aren't that many of them. So I kind of prefer that approach," he says. "As long as they don't change their criteria and say, 'Actually, we need 30,000 of these too.'" But we know that AST's design and technology doesn't need those numbers. Musk does.

An orbital game of Russian roulette

Beyond environmental concerns, there is an even more immediate existential threat: Kessler syndrome. Popularized by the movie Gravity, it is a scenario that keeps space experts like McDowell awake at night. The theory, proposed by NASA scientist Donald Kessler in 1978, describes a domino effect in which a collision between two objects in orbit creates a cloud of debris. Each piece of that debris then becomes a projectile that can cause another collision, creating even more debris, until low Earth orbit becomes an impassable minefield of hypervelocity shrapnel.

"The more satellites you have, the greater the probability of a collision," McDowell states plainly. "And the problem is that once you have the first collision, the debris from it now threatens all the other satellites."

SpaceX has designed a highly automated collision avoidance system for Starlink, and McDowell acknowledges its sophistication. Its satellites constantly monitor their trajectories and can autonomously fire their thrusters to avoid potential impacts. "They perform thousands of maneuvers per month," he says, which is a testament both to the capability of the system and the terribly crowded environment in which it operates. In total, they have performed 50,000 evasive maneuvers since 2019.

But while SpaceX claims its satellites are 100% safe, the facts tell us they are not infallible. "Even with a 99% success rate in deorbiting, a one percent failure rate in a constellation of 30,000 satellites means you're adding 300 dead satellites weighing several hundred kilograms to orbit every five years," McDowell calculates. That's 300 uncontrollable bullets waiting to start the Kessler syndrome.

A catastrophic chain reaction could, in a matter of hours or days, wipe out the essential satellite networks that underpin modern civilization. This isn't just about losing your GPS navigation on the way to a new restaurant. It's about the collapse of global finance, weather forecasting, communications, and critical military and disaster response systems. We are talking about decades of technological regression, a scenario that McDowell finds increasingly plausible as more megaconstellations are launched. It is a high-stakes gamble with the essential infrastructure of civilization.

There is also a danger of direct impact to people on the ground. Some Starlink satellites have already failed in orbit, becoming uncontrollable space debris that fell back to Earth. There is at least one report of a piece of satellite hitting a building in Canada. The latest incident occurred on December 17, 2025, when a Starlink satellite experienced an anomaly, losing communication and causing a propellant tank purge, rapid orbital decay, and the release of debris into low Earth orbit. In a 2023 report to Congress, the FAA warns that there is a real risk that falling Starlink debris could injure or kill someone by 2035.

Space debris is also a problem for rockets. In early November, three taikonauts returned after being stranded at the Chinese international station for nine days. They were unable to use the spacecraft that was to take them back to Earth--the Chengdou-20--because orbital debris had previously struck it. The China Manned Space Agency said the astronauts found "tiny cracks" in a small window on their Shenzhou-20 spacecraft.

The impact was not fatal, but things could have gone very wrong. The Chinese, however, are not acting any differently. Beijing will launch hundreds of thousands of satellites that mimic Starlink's design. They are contributing to the problem and increasing the risk tothemselves and everyone else.

Why AST SpaceMobile can beat Musk

Right now, Starlink does not offer direct broadband to mobile phones; instead, it offers only limited text and data connections. This low-speed connectivity requires a line of sight to the satellite, as SpaceX states on its website. Starlink, despite its leading position in the satellite internet business market, is still trying to catch up on the direct-to-mobile front, and it is very likely that it will never be able to close the gap with AST. Certainly not in the short term, as Musk himself admits.

Musk's company has two huge factors working against it. First is the hardware in orbit. To provide broadband to phones, it needs a next-generation Starlink V3 satellite, which does not yet exist. And even if it did, SpaceX has no way to launch it. With an estimated weight of about 2,000 kilograms, the V3 satellite is too large and heavy for the Falcon 9 workhorse rocket to deploy in economically viable quantities. The entire business model for Starlink V3 dependson the success of Starship, Musk's next-generation super-heavy launchvehicle . But Starship is still in development and has not yet achieved the operational and consistent launch cadence necessary to deploy and maintain a constellation of thousands of V3 satellites.

But even if Musk manages to finish Starship and the Starlink V3 satellites on time, there is a second, even bigger hardware problem: broadband connectivity will not work unless the mobile phone has a special modem chip. Yes, space cadets, you will have to buy a new phone to enjoy Starlink connectivity, while AST works with any current unmodified phone. None of these new Starlink-enabled phones exist or have been announced yet. According to Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's chief operating officer, the company is now working on this chip.

"We are working with chip manufacturers to get the right chips in phones," she told the audience at Space Business Week in Paris last September. Expecting phone manufacturers to incorporate Starlink's proprietary modem into their phones seems like a lot to ask. Especially when manufacturers like Apple have their own plans for mobile-to-space connectivity. It seems unlikely that Tim Cook would tie the company's crown jewel to Musk's whims. Or make phones even more expensive... However,That doesn't even matter because even if Musk had 18,000 of these V3 satellites and Starships ready to launch, the problem would remain the same: you'll need phones with Starlink modems inside them for broadband. And the line-of-sight problem will persist. Broadband only works when the phone can "see" the satellites in the sky.

This is why Musk's initial timeline for direct-to-mobile broadband is entirely speculative. In fact, while Musk said it would be ready in 2026, SpaceX itself admitted that testing of the first phones equipped with Starlink chips is scheduled for 2026, and Starlink aims to complete its constellation of direct-to-mobile V3 satellites in 2027. It is a promise built on a promise, a technological if that depends on a logistical when. Meanwhile, AST SpaceMobile is preparing to launch new operational satellites on existing rockets. Now, Elon Musk himself has admitted that it will take at least two years to get the version 3 satellites into orbit and the phones with that chip. And as experience has shown us time and time again at Tesla, Neuralink, and SpaceX itself, when Musk says two years, it usually translates to six.

AST SpaceMobile has already proven that its technology works, with six operational satellites now transmitting at typical 5G speeds directly to regular phones. This does not mean it has a guaranteed victory against Starlink or any of its competitors. Although it has the capital to execute its plan--backed by investors such as AT&T, Alphabet, Rakuten, Vanguard, BlackRock, and Mexican magnate Carlos Slim, owner of Latin America's largest telecommunications operator--and superior technology, it needs to execute dozens of launches.

This confidence in the technology explains why the stock has soared 333% in a year, but doubts about potential execution problems also explain why the stock experiences wild swings. With every news of a launch or a launch delay, the stock can swing 10% or 20% up or down. That's why the market treats AST as a high-risk, high-reward battleground. It could be a billion-dollar business or explode on the launch pad if the company doesn't get all those satellites up by 2026.

The coup de grâce

This technological and philosophical divergence has not gone unnoticed by Musk. Seeing a direct threat to his ambitions, he has embarked on a campaign to undermine AST SpaceMobile, with baseless accusations, claiming that they are a danger in low Earth orbit due to the size of their satellites. At the same time, Musk is fighting his own problems in low Earth orbit. China has already reported two near-misses with Starlink satellites that caused its Tiangong space station to perform emergency evasive maneuvers. On January 2, SpaceX was forced to move 4,000 satellites into a lower orbit after new research by Chinese scientists highlighted the company's recklessness and the very real risk of collision.

In addition, Musk desperately tried to prevent the FCC from granting AST access to the necessary spectrum--the range of radio frequencies it needs for its satellites to connect to mobile phones on Earth--arguing that it would be "catastrophic" for its service because the powerful signals from AST's large satellites could interfere with Starlink user terminals. In response, AST SpaceMobile claims that its system is designed to coexist with other networks and operates entirely within internationally agreed limits established to prevent such interference. The FCC agreed and allowed AST to use the spectrum. And that move, if every logistical aspect is executed according to plan, gives AST a resounding victory over Musk.

Imagine the radio spectrum as a giant highway in the sky with a limited number of lanes. Carrying data back and forth, AST's trucks have the right to travel on a huge number of these lanes thanks to partners such as AT&T and Verizon. Approximately 35 MHz of what the industry calls the "golden low-band spectrum." It also acquired an extra 45 MHz of low-band spectrum from a bankrupt communications company called Ligado. That's a whopping 80 MHz. And remember the company's proprietary magic formula we mentioned earlier? That's AST's secret weapon for making this highway work, a chip that ties these different radio bands together into a single massive pipe, capable of delivering peak speeds of 120 Mbps to phones, comparable to your typical 5G connection.

SpaceX and its partner T-Mobile have very few lanes available right now: only 5 MHz. That's like comparing an 80-lane superhighway to a 5-lane street. To try to fix that, Musk has spent $17 billion to acquire 50 more lanes: 50 MHz of S-band spectrum from another bankrupt communications company, EchoStar. The problem lies in that "S," which stands for short. Physics dictates that lower frequency radio waves penetrate solid objects more effectively than higher frequency waves. Because L-band waves are longer (lower frequency), they are better at passing through non-metallic obstacles such as walls, foliage, and weather compared to the higher frequency S-band.

That's why Starlink's space-to-mobile service will require line of sight to work. Meanwhile, AST claims that its system will work indoors and outdoors, penetrating buildings in a similar way to a normal mobile signal. Wisniewski claims that a phone will connect through "a wall" and work through the roof of your car due to two factors: they use a low-frequency radio connection, and their satellites are large enough to "hear" and "talk" to phones on the ground even behind obstacles. However, this scenario has not yet been tested by the company or a third party. Only line-of-sight broadband with normal phones has been successfully tested multiple times. If it works inside cars and buildings as he claims, however, the user experience will be seamless. Your phone will simply have service where it didn't before, which will be provided through your existing carrier such as AT&T or Vodafone when it becomes operational sometime in 2026.

Should we really do this?

Scientific evidence and experts tell us that AST has everything it needs to win the next billion-dollar business race. If they execute their plan as they intend, Musk will have a very difficult time competing in space mobile telephony (unlike in home internet connectivity, with his Starlink satellite antennas).

But, whoever wins, should this race even exist? What if we are planning this competition for the wrong reasons?

Maybe we should stop and take a step back. " I hear friends who go on trips to faraway places, look up at the sky, and say, 'Wow, you never see an empty sky anymore,'" McDowell tells me with a touch of sadness and concern. Musk, Bezos, Wisniewski, the Europeans, and the Chinese would argue that we need cheap, ubiquitous internet everywhere in the world, forcivilian and military applications. And of course, there is a lot of money to be made and a genuine need to serve communities in remote locations without having to invest much more money in terrestrial infrastructure, but do we really need to stream TikTok from space?

"I don't necessarily have a position on that," McDowell says. "My position is that even if that's the case, it shouldn't be just the US that decides. It should be decided by all countries around the world because everyone is affected, whether they are space powers or not. And that's the discussion I'm trying to promote: let's have a global conversation, preferably at the UN level, about how to balance the interests of the environment and the space industry more generally."

He's right. And if we all decide that we need this, let's have everyone agree on the best solution to minimize the impact on humanity. The smartest solution. The most technologically advanced.

If we ultimately do this, as a species, let's truly find the smartest and least harmful way, one that doesn't make us all dependent on a man who has shown no consideration for his fellow human beings despite having a savior complex, thinking that only he can guarantee the survival of humanity on a barren red planet.

The fiercest space race is not about returning to the Moon. It's about allowing you to make a TikTok or watch Netflix on your phone anywhere on the planet, from the Atacama salt flats to the Khongor dunes in the Gobi Desert. To make this happen, two radically different design philosophies are at war, and several companies are building the infrastructure necessary to ensure that every phone on the planet is permanently connected to the Internet.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

text:
Africa’s “worst investment destination” just became the testing ground for a billion-dollar bet on beer.

Varun Beverages, the PepsiCo bottler, announced its first push into alcoholic beverages, starting in Zimbabwe with the distribution of Carlsberg beer.

This move challenges Delta's domination in the beer space.

Delta is the largest beverage manufacturer in Zimbabwe. The company holds the Coca-Cola license in the country and also manufactures beer, a segment in which it has been particularly dominant.

Delta holds 96% market share in the beer segment that Varun is now targeting.

Varun Beverages Limited is an Indian-listed bottler for PepsiCo, operating in 10 countries. Its markets include India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and several African nations like Mozambique, Zambia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, which it entered in 2015.

Notably, Zimbabwe is the initial market where Varun is testing beer distribution. This reveals several key dynamics.

➡️First, the risk-to-return trade-off in Zimbabwe is much more attractive than the broader narrative about the country suggests.

While RMB ranked Zimbabwe the worst investment destination in Africa, for Varun, it appears to be one of the first markets worth exploring for this new product category.

Varun has already done very well with its soft drinks business in Zimbabwe after entering in 2015 and is looking to replicate that.

Part of that success was helped by the favourable investment conditions Varun obtained from the Government. This also poses the question: Is there a case to be made that this created unfair competition?

➡️Second, Delta's business must be inherently healthy. When you have both Innscor and Varun Beverages aggressively trying to enter a market—Innscor with its Nyathi beer brand and now Varun with Carlsberg—the unit economics of the business must be strong.

How will Varun's move impact Delta?

There may be a need to unpack this in more detail, but let me leave you with a question that offers a hint.

Varun entered Zimbabwe in 2015 to challenge Delta in the soft drinks market.

Did Delta's beverage sales volumes increase or decline since then?

The answer: Delta's soft drinks volumes between 2016 and 2024 grew at 7.5% per year, even outpacing other parts of the business.

Here's a fascinating paradox: dominant companies often grow when serious competitors emerge, rather than shrink as you'd expect.

Take Econet's data business after Starlink arrived—the pattern holds.

There’s a much deeper story here, one I’ll explore soon.

grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

I’ve put the complaint, the exhibits and the older company records together because I want people to be able to follow this case without having to piece it together from screenshots and replies.

That includes both sides. Korra says he received court documents, denies the allegations and says none of this happened. His denial needs to be included.

X filed its lawsuit against Immortal Snail LLC on September 28, 2026, in the Northern District of Texas. The case number is 4:26-cv-01254. Immortal Snail is the only named defendant in the federal case. Being mentioned in the complaint doesn’t automatically make someone else a defendant.

This is a civil lawsuit about contracts, suspended accounts and arbitration. X wants to stop the arbitration brought by Snail and is suing for breach of contract. There’s no judgment in the material I’ve reviewed establishing the bribery, unauthorized-access or impersonation allegations as proven. The complaint doesn’t bring a standalone RICO claim either, although RICO comes up in an earlier letter.

The complaint itself is 31 pages. The ECF 1 package I reviewed runs to 288 pages, including the cover sheet, index and 25 exhibits. Those exhibits matter because they also include Snail’s account, letters from its lawyers, contracts and commercial records. This package isn’t the entire, up-to-date court file.

One document deserves particular attention: the January 12, 2026 letter from their own lawyers.

Kevin C. Kaplan and Christopher E. Cheek, of Coffey Burlington, say they represent Immortal Snail, Moonrail Limited B.V. and Ossi Ketola. They describe Ketola as the “principal and owner” of both companies. The letter is part of Snail’s arbitration claim, included in Exhibit 25, pages 17–18.

If you have a claim or ongoing proceedings against Ketola involving Duel or CSGOEmpire, that’s a document worth putting in front of your lawyer. It gives them a specific statement from his stated representatives to consider when looking at ownership, corporate relationships and who belongs in your case. The separate companies, directors and representatives have to be considered alongside that statement.

The letter doesn’t settle personal liability, give ownership percentages or establish that one company is a subsidiary of the other. It also doesn’t prove that the companies are fictitious or their directors are acting as fronts. What it does record is how those lawyers described their clients and Ketola’s ownership.

The platforms’ own terms identify the companies:

Duel: Immortal Snail LLC, Nevis, registration L22982.
CSGOEmpire: Moonrail Limited B.V., Curaçao, registration 148182.
Payments for Moonrail may be handled by JHOLT LTD, Cyprus, registration HE393291, under an agreement between the two companies.

Moonrail also appears in DUEL’s trademark records. The official Israeli register lists it as the owner of trademark 374583, registered on May 5, 2025. In Canada, Moonrail filed DUEL application 2342187 on August 6, 2024. The Canadian record names David S. Lipkus of Lipkus Law LLP as the trademark agent and records the application as abandoned under section 36 on July 17, 2026.

That abandonment concerns the Canadian application. It doesn’t mean every DUEL trademark was cancelled or the platform stopped operating. And these records describe different jobs: owning a trademark, operating a platform, processing payments and representing a trademark applicant aren’t interchangeable roles.

The account history in X’s complaint starts in 2024, before the purchases people are discussing.

X alleges that on March 25, 2024, Ketola and Snail took control of an account using @duel, changed its email to a Moonrail mailbox and used it to promote a casino. X says it suspended the account on March 27, after which attempts to recover it involved intermediaries and access to employees. [Paragraphs 36–39.]

X also alleges that Ketola and CSGOEmpire were involved in an intrusion into @CSGORoll reported in April 2024. It cites a livestream in which, according to the complaint, Ketola celebrated what happened, mentioned “Sticky Hand” and said he worked for him. I haven’t authenticated the original video. X says it suspended @JNSAST the following day after reports of targeted harassment, disclosure of personal information and threats. [Paragraphs 28–29.]

The complaint goes on to describe what X calls bribery and unauthorized account reinstatements. It alleges that internal information about @duel was obtained in June 2024 and usernames were changed to move @monarch to another account. It also says an employee photographed internal information in July after a $1,500 offer and was fired. Further reinstatements through contractors and further suspensions followed, according to X. [Paragraphs 39, 40 and 44–49.]

There’s a company letter in this part of the file too. Exhibit 3 contains Moonrail’s July 9, 2024 authorization for Dušan Pećić to represent it. The names beneath the signatures are Lorenza Godett and Christopher van Rosberg, acting for Xecutive Corporate Management B.V., which is identified as a director of Moonrail. HLTV also named Pećić as CSGOEmpire’s marketing manager in March 2024.

The letter authorizes representation. It doesn’t authorize hacking, bribery or threats, or show that its signatories knew about the conduct X alleges.

The dates also need to stay as written. X dates Pećić’s appeal to June 28, 2024, but the authorization letter is dated July 9. Paragraph 47 then dates the rejection to July 13, 2025. I’m not going to quietly change those dates to make them line up.

Haci Isik appears as an intermediary. X says he was engaged in December 2024 to recover @duel and looked for insiders willing to reactivate or suspend accounts for money. It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Part of the dispute is which terms apply. The 2024 handle-transfer terms select a Texas forum, reserve suspension rights and include a $100 limit on liability. Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

Madan Lal Dhingra is hanged to death on this date in 1909 in London. A great revolutionary, close associate of Veer Savarkar, whose story needs to be known more.

Early Life

Hailing from Amritsar, the sixth born of the city’s Civil Surgeon, two of his brothers were doctors, while two other were barristers.  Coming from a well to do and influential family, Dhingra, could have settled into a life of luxury and comfort.

Yet he was restless, driven by the call for Swadeshi, right from his student days at the Government College, Lahore in 1904. He led the student protest there against having to forcibly wear a blazer made of imported cloth, which led to his expulsion in turn.

Having extensively studied about poverty and famines in India,  he felt that only Swaraj( Self Government) was the solution. For some time, he worked as a clerk at a Tanga service in Kalka, Shimla, where his attempts to organize an union came to nought.

London

It was then on the advice of his brother, he went to London, for studying the Diploma Course in Civil Engineering at University College between 1906-09.  A very illustrious institution of learning where Dadabhai Naoroji  taught and Tagore was a student.

Like most other Indian students in England, he was a regular to the India House founded by Shyamji Krishna Verma. His initial days, were spent in frolic and fun, and his good looks ensured, he was in the company of women mostly.

Veer Savarkar

The turning point came, at a meeting in India House that was addressed by Savarkar. Apparently Dhingra along with his friends, was making a noise in the adjacent room, that forced Savarkar to intervene.

"What is the matter? You only talk of action and bravery, avoid coming to our weekly meetings. Is this your bravery”

The rebuke by Savarkar had it’s desired effect, and for quite some time Dhingra was not seen around India House. Too ashamed to show his face, and fearful of facing Savarkar’s wrath, he kept away. Until one day, summoning all the courage, he came face to face with Savarkar again at India House.

Savarkar however had moved on from the past incident, and spoke normally with Dhingra.  A much assured Dhingra asked him 

“Has the time for sacrifice come?”.

And then Savarkar gave one of the best replies ever

“If you have made up your mind and are ready, it is generally understood that the time for sacrifice has come.”

This would guide Dhingra's course of action.

Having made up his mind, Dhingra now joined the National Indian Association, founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose in 1876, Dhingra acted as a double agent of sorts, publicly denouncing Savarkar in front of the British, to win their favor.

 He soon won the trust of Ms.Emma Josephine Beck, the secretary of the Association, and got to know the timings of visits of important officials.

Assasination of Curzon Wylie

Wylie was one of the top ranking officers in the British Government and eaded, the Secret Police, a fact not known to any one, except those in the upper echelons of the British Government. He in turn, was keeping an eye on Savarkar and other revolutionaries at the Indian House.

He even appointed an informer, Kirtikar at the Indian House, to get information. Kirtikar was however found out by Savarkar, and gave him all the information about the police operations under force.

Dhingra knew Wylie personally, having met him earlier on April 13, 1909 based on a recommendation from his brother Kundan Lal.  Dhingra apparently wanted to discuss the letter, but in reality his aim was to get closer to Wylie, win his confidence.

Dhingra met Savarkar on June 29,1909 at Bipin Chandra Pal’s home in London,  discussed the plans of the assassination with him.

 Savarkar asked Niranjan Pal to type out the statement, Dhingra would make after the assassination, and then gave him a Belgian make Browning pistol. And told him as he took leave.

“Do not show me your face again if you fail this time” 

Accompanied by another revolutionary Koregaonkar, he had an early lunch and tea, left at 2 PM, cradling the revolver in his hands. 

He also bought a brand new dagger in a leather casket, placing it in his pocket.  It was evening 7 PM, when the function started, Dhingra was dressed in a lounge suit and blue Punjab turban.

He placed a Colt revolver in the right pocket of his coat, and the Browning gifted by Savarkar in another. He took a cab, arrived at the Institute, where Koregaonkar came also, with his pistol. When the time came for Wylie to leave, Dhingra approached him on the pretext of talking something.

Just at the landing, coming closer to Wylie, Dhingra pulled out his Colt and fired two bullets point blank.  As Wylie reeled, Dhingra fired two more bullets, a Parsi doctor, Cawas Lalkaka, who tried to save Wylie  was also shot.

Arrest and Trial

Dhingra’s plan to commit suicide however failed , as he was overpowered by the security guards around.  He managed to even bring down one of the guards, but was ultimately subdued, and arrested.  

He was taken to the Walton Street Police Station, where the Police Officer asked him if any of his friends knew about this. To which Dhingra calmly replied

 “There is no need, they will know about my arrest tomorrow in the newspapers”. 

It was a smart strategy, which ensured none of his friends would be implicated. 

Sadly Dhingra was disowned by his own family itself. His brother Bhajan Lal, who was in London, condemned him publicly in a meeting. His father publicly apologized and disowned his son.

All his family members dropped Dhingra from their surname and adopted Lal, to avoid trouble with the British. The only person who actually stood by Madan Lal Dhingra was Savarkar, who visited him in prison.

He was emotionally overwhelmed, when Savarkar told him 

“I have come here to seek your darshan”. 

For some one disowned by his family, it meant a lot that somebody out there still cared for him.

The Indian Association held a public meeting on July 5, 1909 to condemn Dhingra’s assassination of Wylie. The meeting was chaired by Aga Khan, and as he was prepared to pass the resolution, one hand raised in protest.

It was Savarkar who said

“No, not unanimously. There are opponents of the motion as well. Take down my name, Savarkar. I oppose the motion.”

August 17, 1909, Pentonville Prison.

Finally the date had come, many of Dhingra’s friends made a request to meet him for one last time. JS Master, made a request to the Under Sheriff of London and Home Office, stating he was Dhingra’s close friend and needed to meet him.

Dhingra however remained calm and composed, slept well on his last night, and after performing his chores, was ready for the hanging. As the clock struck nine, he walked to the gallows.

When a Christian preacher Hudson, walked up to him, for the last prayer, Dhingra turned him down, saying he was born as a Hindu and would die as one. Metcalfe, the Dy. Under Sheriff of London, read out the death warrant to Dhingra, asked him the usual questions.

Dhingra just ignored, walked calmly to the noose, to Officer Pierpoint who was waiting for him there. The noose was put around his neck, and the levers pulled, the life of a brave revolutionary was snuffed out.

Dhingra's statement during the Trial and and "Challenge" his full statement just before he was hanged. Powerful words.

Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
India's platforms are legally required to notify users when their content gets taken down by government order — but compliance is spotty at best.
The rule exists under the Information Technology Act's intermediary framework. When a platform receives a government takedown notice, users are supposed to get an explanation: what was removed, why, and which authority issued it.
In practice, most platforms either ignore this entirely or send vague notices after the fact. No timeline is enforced. No standardized format exists. Users often discover their content is gone only when they try to access it.
Former MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) cyber-law officials have flagged this gap repeatedly. The logic was simple: transparency about state censorship creates a paper trail, deters overreach, and lets users contest removals.
But India's digital ecosystem treats the notification rule as optional. WhatsApp doesn't notify for group bans. Twitter (now X) batches notices weeks later. YouTube compliance varies by region. TikTok, before its ban, rarely proactively informed users.
The enforcement gap matters because:
• There is no penalty structure — platforms face no fines or license consequences for skipping notification.
• Users have no realistic way to challenge removals without knowing they happened or why.
• Government agencies know the lack of oversight means takedowns go undocumented.
• A parallel system of private censorship operates without the judicial review that formal bans would trigger.
The fix would require either stricter intermediary rules with real penalties, or a centralized notification registry — both politically difficult in India's current regulatory environment.
As government content moderation requests accelerate globally, India's notification gap is becoming a template for how to make state censorship functionally invisible.
